raw_case_text:
A 31-year-old man was evaluated in the emergency room (ER) of our institution for persistent diarrhea of 3 weeks duration. He also reported abdominal pain along with lightheadedness. He described the abdominal pain as vague, diffuse, nonradiating, and mild in intensity without any precipitating or relieving factors. He reported up to 10 episodes of watery diarrhea which did not contain any blood. He also complained of fever and dysuria. About 3 weeks before the current presentation, the patient had presented to the ER with dysuria, abdominal pain, and intermittent diarrhea. At that time he was admitted and treated for a urinary tract infection (UTI) with ciprofloxacin and later discharged home. As per patient, his diarrhea had worsened after taking the antibiotics and had presented with the current symptoms. There was no nausea, vomiting, constipation, fever, and early satiety or appetite changes. He had a prior history of HIV/AIDS, had not been adherent to antiretroviral therapy or PCP prophylaxis. He had a high viral load and low CD4 count.
He was a current smoker and admitted smoking 4 or more cigarettes per day but denied using alcohol except on social occasions or illicit drugs. He did not have a family history of liver, stomach, or colon cancer. His medications included acetaminophen and ciprofloxacin.
On examination, he was found to have a temperature of 39.1 C, blood pressure of 108/52 mmHg, a pulse rate of 99 beats per minute, and a respiratory rate of 16 breaths per minute. The patient was alert, fully oriented, and communicative. The abdomen was scaphoid, nontender, and nondistended with normal bowel sounds. There was no palpable hepatomegaly; however, the spleen was palpable. Shotty cervical and inguinal lymph nodes were palpated. The rest of the physical examination was unremarkable.
Routine laboratory tests showed a hemoglobin level of 8 g/dL, white blood cell count of 3.7 k/uL, serum potassium level of 3.4 mEq/L, and albumin level of 1.7 g/dL. Stool studies including Clostridium difficile cytotoxin, fecal leucocyte stain, and fecal fat were negative. His blood and stool cultures were negative for the growth of Mycobacterium avium complex. A chest X-ray revealed a right lower lobe consolidation and bilateral pleural effusions. The patient was initiated on broad spectrum antibiotics for hospital-acquired infection. A CT of the chest was done as a part of workup revealed moderate right and small left pleural effusions, consolidation in the dependent lung bases, nodular opacities in both lungs, some cavitary in nature, and patchy ground glass opacity in both lungs (Figure 1). Sputum for acid-fast bacilli (AFB) was negative, ruling out pulmonary tuberculosis. CT abdomen and pelvis done for chronic diarrhea and abdominal pain revealed a hypodense lesion within the cephalad aspect of the spleen, a 6.7 cm splenic mass with adjacent small nodule, multiple hypodense hepatic lesions, measuring up to 12 mm in diameter, and mild ascites in the upper abdomen (Figure 2). Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) abdomen showed a heterogeneous lesion within the upper pole of the spleen measuring 5.2 x 4.3 cm in size with absent enhancement centrally, with some enhancement along the peripheral aspect of the lesion, suggesting central necrosis (Figure 3). He underwent an ultrasound-guided core biopsy with an 18-gauge (18G) needle. Two core biopsies were obtained for histologic analysis of the splenic mass. The histopathology revealed necrotizing granulomas on hematoxylin and eosin stain (Figures 4 and 5) with Pneumocystis jirovecii infection on Grocott-Gomori's methenamine silver (GMS) stain (Figures 6(a) and 6(b)). A fiberoptic bronchoscopy with transbronchial biopsy was also done revealing P. jirovecii pneumonia, while bronchoalveolar lavage was negative for malignant cells. His alpha fetoprotein (AFP) level was 3.2 ng/ml. Results of the rest of the laboratory parameters are given in Table 1. The patient was started on sulfamethoxazole with trimethoprim, and no steroids were given. Antiretroviral therapy was not started at the time of discharge due to concerns over IRS (immune reconstitution syndrome). He continued to follow-up at our hospital as an outpatient.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 31-year-old man with untreated HIV/AIDS presented to the emergency department with a 3-week history of persistent watery diarrhea, vague diffuse abdominal pain, lightheadedness, fever, and dysuria.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Three weeks prior to current presentation, the patient had been admitted via the emergency room for dysuria, abdominal pain, and intermittent diarrhea, and was discharged on oral ciprofloxacin for a urinary tract infection. Following antibiotic treatment, his watery nonbloody diarrhea worsened to up to 10 episodes daily accompanied by mild diffuse abdominal pain, lightheadedness, fever, and persistent dysuria. He had a known history of HIV/AIDS with high viral load and low CD4 count and was nonadherent to antiretroviral therapy and PCP prophylaxis.
subjective.past_medical_history: HIV/AIDS with nonadherence to antiretroviral therapy and PCP prophylaxis; urinary tract infection treated 3 weeks prior with ciprofloxacin. Social history: Current smoker (>=4 cigarettes/day), social alcohol use, no illicit drug use; negative family history of GI malignancy.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for watery nonbloody diarrhea (up to 10 episodes/day), vague diffuse abdominal pain, lightheadedness, fever, and dysuria; negative for nausea, vomiting, constipation, early satiety, or appetite changes. Recent medications were ciprofloxacin and acetaminophen.

objective.physical_examination: Admission vital signs: Temperature 39.1 °C, blood pressure 108/52 mmHg, pulse 99 beats/min, and respiratory rate 16 breaths/min. Physical exam: Alert, oriented, and communicative; scaphoid, nontender, nondistended abdomen with normal bowel sounds, palpable splenomegaly, and no hepatomegaly; shotty cervical and inguinal lymphadenopathy.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission laboratory tests: Anemia with hemoglobin 8.0 g/dL, leukopenia with WBC 3.7 K/μL, hypokalemia with serum potassium 3.4 mEq/L, severe hypoalbuminemia with albumin 1.7 g/dL, and alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) 3.2 ng/mL. Stool and microbiological studies: Negative Clostridioides difficile cytotoxin, fecal leukocyte stain, and fecal fat; blood and stool cultures negative for Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC); sputum smears negative for acid-fast bacilli (AFB). Admission chest X-ray: Right lower lobe consolidation and bilateral pleural effusions.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest CT scan: Moderate right and small left pleural effusions, dependent basilar consolidations, bilateral nodular opacities (some cavitary), and bilateral patchy ground-glass opacities. Abdominopelvic CT and abdominal MRI: Multiple hypodense hepatic lesions (up to 12 mm), mild upper abdominal ascites, and a large centrally necrotic upper-pole splenic mass (6.7 cm on CT; 5.2 x 4.3 cm on MRI with peripheral enhancement) plus an adjacent small splenic nodule. Ultrasound-guided 18G core needle biopsy of the splenic mass and fiberoptic bronchoscopy with transbronchial lung biopsy: Both splenic core biopsy and transbronchial lung biopsy demonstrated necrotizing granulomas on H&E and abundant Pneumocystis jirovecii organisms on Grocott-Gomori methenamine silver (GMS) staining (BAL negative for malignancy).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Disseminated Pneumocystis jirovecii infection presenting with cavitary/nodular Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, hepatosplenic pneumocystosis (necrotizing granulomatous 6.7 cm splenic mass and multiple hepatic lesions), and chronic diarrhea in a nonadherent patient with advanced HIV/AIDS, definitively confirmed by Grocott-Gomori methenamine silver (GMS) staining on both ultrasound-guided splenic core biopsy and transbronchial lung biopsy. Plan and clinical course: Treated with oral/IV trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole without adjunctive corticosteroids (and with antiretroviral therapy temporarily deferred at discharge to avoid immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome), followed by outpatient infectious disease follow-up.
